title: It speaks like an adult before it speaks like a child
body: #1 has lived its first 72 months. Before it heard anything it produced random characters. At 12 months it already strings real words together, and from then on it talks in whole adult sentences: asked “do you want to play with the ball?”, the 18-month snapshot answers “we wanted to play with you today”.

Real children are nowhere near this. Counting only real words, #1 at 12 months says 3.5 words per utterance; children of the same age in the same recordings say 0.9. At 18 months it is 4.4 against 1.5; at 36 months 5.0 against 3.4.

The reason is how it was raised. It only ever heard adults talking to children, so the first thing it learns to imitate is an adult. The short, telegraphic speech of a two-year-old does not grow out of learning from this input alone. Whatever produces it — a body, a world, a mind that cannot yet hold a long sentence — is missing from #1.

title: The first copy
body: The lineage starts by copying. Grown #1 copies, word by word, everything adults said to children in its own upbringing. At each word it lapses with probability 5% and writes the word it expects instead of the one in front of it. Its copy will raise the next generation.

In a first test on 800 lines, 82% came through unchanged. A lapse is the parent's own guess, so it leans towards what the parent expects: rare words often turn into common ones (“ball” became “beautiful”, “telephones” became “and”), and agreement can shift (“when are you gonna bring em home” became “when is you gonna bring em home”). Whether these drifts pile up over generations is what the lineage is for.

correction: Correction (see 20261028-03): on the full copy, “rare words often turn into common ones” does not hold beyond what any word swap would do. The examples were picked from a small test.

title: Correction: the lapses do not favour common words
body: The full first copy is done: 800,527 lines, 82% unchanged, 180,335 lapses. Entry 20261028-02 said that a lapse leans towards common words. That came from a handful of examples, and it does not survive a fair comparison.

The comparison is a null model: at every lapse, instead of letting #1 write a word, draw a word at random by how often it occurs in the original. Any swap pulls a rare word towards commoner ones, simply because most words drawn are common; that is regression to the mean, not a property of the copyist.

Measured against this null, #1 pulls rare words upward slightly less than random swapping does, and pulls frequent words downward slightly less too. Its replacements stay closer to the frequency of the word they replace. What #1 does at a lapse looks more like finding a word that fits the context than like reaching for a common one. It also invented 7,479 non-words.

title: A slip the next generation repeats? (a hint, not a finding)
body: #4, #5 and #6 are grown. They are the first children of the lineage: same learner and same upbringing as #1, #2 and #3, same seeds, but instead of the original recordings they heard #1's copy of them, in which 5% of words were written #1's own way.

Some of #1's lapses broke agreement between subject and verb: “when are you gonna bring em home” became “when is you gonna bring em home”. Phrases like “are he” do not occur in the original at all; #1's copy has 14 of them.

When the children speak, these mismatches turn up a little more often than in their parents' generation. #4 says “where are he going” and “what are he doing”. Over all the speech each generation produced (about 58,000 utterances per individual), “are he” appears 15 times in the children against 5 in the parents, “is we” 13 against 4, “are it” 7 against 2.

This is a hint, not a result. The counts are tiny, some matches are ordinary sentences, and there is no comparison yet with a null model or with a second generation. The real test comes when #4 copies the book it grew up with: if the mismatches it learned make its own lapses lean the same way, the slip has started to spread.
update: Tested in 20261104-04: children say their own parent's slips more often than children raised on another copy do.

title: Word endings come early; agreement stays shaky
body: Every monthly snapshot of #1–#9 was given 441 pairs of sentences that differ in one point of grammar, and later 4,600 pairs from the 23 test types of the Zorro battery. A snapshot passes a pair when it prefers the grammatical sentence more than it did at 0 months, before hearing anything. A test type counts as learnt at 80%, held for three snapshots in a row.

Regular past tense is learnt at 12–15 months. Subject–verb agreement stays near 70%: only #2 and #3 pass it, at 36 months. Irregular past drops below chance at 8–12 months and climbs back to about 0.7. That is over-regularisation and recovery, without the earlier phase of correct, memorised forms that children show.

Nonce plurals look learnt early, but the same snapshots also add -s where it does not belong: at 12 months they choose the wrong plural on singular items most of the time. Early on this is a liking for the suffix, not a rule.

On Zorro, 6 or 7 of the 23 test types are passed at 144 months. Four of those are already passed at 6 months, after half a year of input, so local word strings are probably enough for them. Counting only test types passed later, all of #1–#3 learn two: nominative pronouns (at 12 months) and agreement across a local attractor (16–30 months).

title: A bigger learner and doubled input did not teach more grammar
body: If the grammar #1–#3 miss is a matter of size, a larger learner should pass more. #13–#15 are 2.4 times larger (25.4M parameters) and heard the same input. At 72 months they pass 3, 2 and 3 Zorro test types, not counting those passed at 6 months; #1–#3 pass 3, 3 and 2. The larger learner fits its training input better and held-out speech worse (1.87 against 1.72 bits per character): it memorises.

If it is a matter of input, more of the right sentences should help. #16–#27 heard Ω with one kind of sentence doubled, taken from other families' recordings: determiner–noun sentences, negative polarity items, or irregular past. A fourth group heard the same amount of random sentences. No group beat the random group on its own test type, and the nominative pronouns already learnt held in every group.

Both tests are weaker than they look. The irregular-verb test compares “had grown” with “had grew”, and the added sentences were mostly simple past. The negative-polarity test turns on sentence-initial “only”, and the added sentences brought in one more of those. Only the determiner test matched what was added.

title: Books alone erase conversation; three parts in ten of talk keep it
body: #1–#3 went to school at 72 months: children's books from Project Gutenberg, easy to hard, about a million words a year up to 144 months, and nothing else. The books were learnt: on held-out book text the loss fell from 3.17 to 2.22 bits per character by 108 months. Conversation went. On held-out adult speech the loss rose from 1.73 to 2.64 after six months of books, and to about 3.3 by 144 months.

#10–#12 are clones of #1–#3 at 72 months. They read the same books with 30% family speech mixed in. Conversation held, and the books were learnt just as well (2.35 bits per character on held-out book text at 144 months, the same as the books-only group).

The forgetting is selective. In the books-only group question agreement fell back to chance, while irregular past, common in storybook narration, improved from about 0.5 to 0.8. One caveat: the mixed-in speech came from months 36–72, which the held-out speech may resemble, so the mixed group's score may be flattering.

title: Children inherit their parent's slips
body: Entry 20261028-04 noticed that a few agreement slips in #1's copy came back in #4–#6. This is the test. A variant is a word pair that a parent's copy brought in: it occurs at most twice in Ω and at least five times in the copy. #1's copy has 168 variants of its own, #2's has 140, #3's has 127.

#7–#9 were raised on #2's copy, as #4–#6 were on #1's. Each group says its own parent's variants more often than the other group does: cross ratio 2.51 (95% interval 1.70–3.80, permutation p = 0.0005). #3 has no children, so its variants serve as a control, and they show no difference (0.83, interval 0.61–1.16). Taken alone, the #2 branch is weaker (1.34, interval 0.98–1.85).
The effect grows with exposure. Against the parent generation, #4–#6 say a variant 2.05 times as often when it occurs 5–9 times in #1's copy, and 5.82 times as often when it occurs 20 times or more.
